name: United States Declaration of Independence
info: The Declaration of Independence is the founding document of the United States, adopted by the Second Continental Congress in Philadelphia on 4 July 1776, explaining why the Thirteen Colonies regarded themselves as independent states no longer under British rule.

facts.made: Drafted largely by Thomas Jefferson between 11 and 28 June 1776 for the Committee of Five, then edited and adopted by the Second Continental Congress; the signed copy was engrossed by the clerk Timothy Matlack
facts.form: A political and legal statement, often discussed as five parts: introduction, preamble, indictment of King George III, denunciation of the British people and conclusion; it lists 27 grievances against the king
facts.where: The signed, engrossed copy is on display at the National Archives in Washington, D.C.; two Dunlap broadsides are kept in the Library of Congress
facts.known: The words 'all men are created equal'; 'Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness'; Jefferson's drafting; the 27 grievances; the Dunlap broadside; John Hancock's signature; the struck-out passage on the slave trade; its later use by reform movements

t: Congress voted for independence on 2 July 1776 and approved the wording of the Declaration on 4 July; Thomas Jefferson wrote most of the first draft, and Congress cut nearly a fourth of it.
It gave the political, moral and legal grounds for independence, citing 27 grievances against King George III and asserting natural and legal rights, including a right of revolution.
Little noticed in the years after the Revolution, it gained a second life from the 1790s and was later invoked by abolitionists, women's rights campaigners, Abraham Lincoln and many new states.
dyk: Jefferson's draft charged King George III with forcing the slave trade on the colonies, but Congress struck the passage out, in part to appease South Carolina and Georgia, which had significant involvement in the slave trade. Jefferson later wrote that Congress had 'mangled' his draft.
ev: The American Revolutionary War begins in April with the battles of Lexington and Concord, and the Second Continental Congress meets in Philadelphia in May
On 11 June Congress appoints the Committee of Five, and Jefferson writes the first draft between 11 and 28 June
On 2 July Congress adopts the resolution of independence, and on 4 July it approves the final wording of the Declaration and sends it to the printer
John Dunlap's broadsides are read in public on 8 July in Philadelphia, Trenton and Easton, and most delegates sign the engrossed copy on 2 August
A facsimile of the engrossed copy is made, and it becomes the basis of most modern reproductions
The Seneca Falls Convention issues a Declaration of Sentiments patterned on the Declaration, with the words 'all men and women are created equal'
Abraham Lincoln makes the Declaration the centrepiece of his Gettysburg Address
The engrossed Declaration is transferred to the National Archives, where it is on permanent display

sections.origins:
By July 1776 the Thirteen Colonies and Great Britain had been at war for over a year. Relations had been worsening since 1763, and Parliament's measures to raise revenue, including the Stamp Act of 1765 and the Townshend Acts, met the argument that Parliament, in which the colonies were not directly represented, had no right to tax them. The orthodox British view, dating from the Glorious Revolution of 1688, held Parliament supreme throughout the empire, while in the colonies the idea had grown that the British Constitution recognised fundamental rights no government could violate. By 1774 writers such as Samuel Adams, James Wilson and Thomas Jefferson argued that Parliament was the legislature of Great Britain only.

After the Coercive Acts of 1774, the First Continental Congress organised a boycott and petitioned the king. The war began in April 1775, yet most colonists still hoped for reconciliation until the king rejected a second petition and issued a Proclamation of Rebellion in 1775. Thomas Paine's Common Sense appeared in January 1776 and opened a public debate on independence. Congress could not act at will: delegates were bound by instructions from their colonies, and between April and July 1776 a 'complex political war' was waged to have these revised. Historian Pauline Maier counts more than ninety local declarations of independence in those months.
sections.content:
The Declaration is not divided into formal sections, but it is often discussed as five parts: an introduction, a preamble, an indictment of King George III, a denunciation of the British people and a conclusion. It justified the independence of the colonies by citing 27 grievances against the king and by asserting certain natural and legal rights, including a right of revolution. Its second sentence holds that 'all men are created equal' and are endowed by their Creator with unalienable rights, among them 'Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness'.

Historians disagree about what kind of document it is. John Phillip Reid argued that it is less a philosophical tract on natural rights than a legal indictment of the king for violating the constitutional rights of the colonists. David Armitage argued that its primary purpose was to express the international legal sovereignty of the United States, since the revolutionaries had to show they were no longer dependent on Great Britain if European powers were to recognise them. The Declaration does not have the force of law domestically, but it may help to provide historical and legal clarity about the Constitution and other laws.

Jefferson's own draft included a passage condemning the slave trade and blaming King George III for it. Congress deleted it, so it does not appear in the final text.
sections.making:
On 7 June 1776 Richard Henry Lee, following instructions from the Virginia Convention, presented a resolution that the colonies 'are, and of right ought to be, free and independent States'. Congress postponed the debate for three weeks and, on 11 June, appointed the Committee of Five: John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Thomas Jefferson, Robert R. Livingston and Roger Sherman. The committee took no minutes, and the accounts later written by Jefferson and Adams contradict each other. What is certain is that Adams persuaded the committee to choose Jefferson as the writer. Jefferson largely wrote the draft between 11 and 28 June in a rented house at 700 Market Street in Philadelphia, and the committee presented its copy to Congress on 28 June.

His most immediate sources were his own draft of the preamble of the Constitution of Virginia and George Mason's draft of the Virginia Declaration of Rights. Scholars disagree about wider influences: John Locke is usually cited, but others stress Jean Jacques Burlamaqui, Francis Hutcheson, republicanism or de Vattel's The Law of Nations. Jefferson himself wrote in 1825 that it was not aiming at originality and was meant to be 'an expression of the American mind'.

Congress edited the draft for two days, shortening it by a fourth. It voted on independence on 1 July, when nine delegations voted yes, and on 2 July, when twelve voted yes and New York abstained. It approved the final wording on 4 July.
sections.reception:
John Dunlap printed about 200 broadsides on the night of 4 July. The Pennsylvania Evening Post published the text on 6 July, and it was read publicly on 8 July at noon in Philadelphia, Trenton and Easton. George Washington had it read to his troops in New York City on 9 July, and in many cities crowds tore down signs and statues of royal authority; a statue of King George in New York City was pulled down and its lead made into musket balls. The text reached British newspapers from mid-August, Florence and Warsaw by mid-September, and France in November 1776.

The North Ministry gave no official answer, but secretly commissioned John Lind to publish an Answer to the Declaration of the American Congress, and Thomas Hutchinson, the former royal governor of Massachusetts, also published a rebuttal. Hutchinson argued that the Revolution was the work of a few conspirators. Lind's pamphlet carried an attack on natural rights by Jeremy Bentham. Both asked how slaveholders in Congress could proclaim that all men are created equal without freeing their own slaves.

In late November 1776 a group of 547 Loyalists, largely from New York, signed a Declaration of Dependence pledging loyalty to the Crown. The Spanish-American authorities banned the Declaration, but it was widely translated and passed on.
sections.survival:
Delegates knew that signing was an act of high treason, which was punishable by torture and death. Congress resolved on 19 July to have the Declaration engrossed on parchment under the title 'The unanimous declaration of the thirteen United States of America'. The clerk Timothy Matlack probably engrossed it, and most delegates signed it on 2 August 1776; fifty-six signatures are affixed. Thomas McKean disputed in 1796 that it was signed on 4 July, and historians have generally accepted his version. The Dunlap broadside is also regarded as an official text by Julian P. Boyd, who argued that the Declaration, like Magna Carta, is not a single document. Of about 200 broadsides printed, 26 are known to survive, the last found in The National Archives in England in 2009.

The engrossed copy was poorly conserved in the 19th century, and much of its ink had faded by 1876; a facsimile of 1823 became the basis of most modern reproductions. Custody passed from the State Department to the Library of Congress in 1921. After the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941 it was moved to Fort Knox until 1944, and in 1952 it went to the National Archives. A second engrossed copy, the 'Sussex Declaration', was announced in 2017 in West Sussex, England; how it got there is not yet known. Jefferson's 'original Rough draught' survives, but the first draft and the copy submitted to Congress on 28 June were lost.
sections.legacy:
The Declaration received little attention in the years after the Revolution: early Independence Day celebrations and histories largely ignored it, and it was rarely mentioned in the debates over the Constitution. Interest revived in the 1790s, when Jeffersonian Republicans promoted it and Jefferson as its author while Federalists emphasised the whole Congress. After the War of 1812 it gained a wider following, and from the 1820s variations of it were issued to proclaim the rights of workers, farmers and women, among them the Seneca Falls Convention's Declaration of Sentiments of 1848.

Its relation to slavery was debated from the start. Abolitionists such as William Lloyd Garrison treated it as a founding text alongside the Bible, while defenders of slavery such as John C. Calhoun argued that 'all men are created equal' was false or did not apply to black people. Abraham Lincoln read it as setting a standard for all men, as in his Peoria speech of 1854 and the Gettysburg Address of 1863; Pauline Maier judged Stephen Douglas's narrower reading more historically accurate, but Lincoln's view prevailed.

Abroad, the French Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789) drew on it, and David Armitage argues that it began a genre of declarations of independence, whose later examples include Venezuela (1811), Liberia (1847) and Vietnam (1945).

summary: The Declaration of Independence explained why the Thirteen Colonies saw themselves as independent states, listing 27 grievances against King George III. Adopted on 4 July 1776 and drafted largely by Jefferson, it was little noticed at first, then became a standard for movements and new states.
references: David Armitage, The Declaration of Independence: A Global History (Harvard University Press, 2007)
Carl Lotus Becker, The Declaration of Independence: A Study in the History of Political Ideas (Harcourt, Brace and Company, 1922)
Pauline Maier, American Scripture: Making the Declaration of Independence (Vintage Books, 1998)
Dumas Malone, The Story of the Declaration of Independence (Oxford University Press, 1954)
Alexander Tsesis, For Liberty and Equality: The Life and Times of the Declaration of Independence (Oxford University Press, 2012)
notes: The article's discussion of the Declaration's five parts gives no section text, so the content section describes the structure and its two disputed readings only.

The article gives the vote of 1 July (nine delegations in favour) and the adoption of the resolution on 2 July with twelve votes; the final wording is approved on 4 July. All three are given as the article has them.
The article says 'the first formal public readings' were on 8 July at three places and also that Washington had it read on 9 July; both given.

The article's bibliography and references sections are empty in the saved text, and the Further reading entries are recent books and a magazine essay not otherwise cited, so references are left empty for the editor.
The article says both that the committee presented its copy on 28 June and that this copy was lost; I gave only the loss.

Left out: tourism-style, film, game and currency uses; the Trump Oval Office copy of 2025; One World Trade Center; the apocryphal signing anecdotes; Brown's Declaration of Liberty; the Black Panther and Harvey Milk quotations.

The article says the Declaration was 'unanimously ratified' on 4 July and also tells of New York abstaining on 2 July (allowed to vote a week later); the text gives the vote as the article does for 2 July and does not repeat 'unanimous' for the vote itself.
The Dunlap broadside count: about 200 printed, 26 known to survive, as in the article.
